subtitle: Make sure your message comes through in speech, sound and visuals, then review the alternatives you provide and how the video or audio is delivered.
scope: Learning is voluntary. The course uses complete original practice content and prototype observations; no actual recording, player or individual is tested. Applicable standards, information, permission, assistance, publication and agency responsibilities remain. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: A recording can play while someone still misses an important instruction, sound or visual choice. Explore a short message, find a caption error that changes its meaning and consider how description and transcripts can help. Then examine the player tasks and what still needs checking. Work with the example at your own pace; you can keep your reflections private.

lessons.title: Identify the message in sound and images
lessons.summary: Begin with what the recording communicates through speech, other sound and visible information. The media type and actual content guide the alternatives to examine.
lessons.objective: Identify the supplied speech, sound and visual information in the practice recording.
objectives: Identify the supplied speech, sound and visual information in the practice recording.
Distinguish prerecorded audio-only, silent video and synchronized audio-video.
Choose a planning question that retains the message rather than assuming one feature covers it.
takeaways: Different channels can carry different information.
Media type affects the relevant alternatives.
A file’s existence does not establish usable content.
lessons.statement: Identify where the important meaning is before choosing an alternative.

intro.heading: What does the practice recording communicate?
intro.body:
In this example, Elva and Niko are DHS colleagues planning a prerecorded practice video about preparing for an optional discussion. The recording contains three important pieces of information. Elva says, No decision is needed today; choose a question to discuss. The image shows a card titled Questions with two choices, Timing and Wording. A short chime accompanies the move from that card to a closing screen. In this example the chime signals the change of screen rather than a decision or approval.

Use this example to explore how the message reaches people through speech, sound and images. The spoken instruction supplies the optional discussion task. The visible choices tell a person what questions are available. The relevant sound marks a transition. Neither the filename nor the fact that a recording plays answers whether all of those pieces can be understood through the available alternatives.

A prerecorded audio-only item has no video information to describe. A silent video has visible information but no speech to caption. The main practice video combines audio and moving images, so its speech, relevant sound and important visual content each deserve attention. Naming those differences prevents Elva from choosing an alternative only because it was used for a different kind of file.

WCAG 2.1 distinguishes requirements for these media types and for live or prerecorded content, with specified conditions and exceptions. Minnesota’s adopted digital standard retains its actual scope and applicable responsibilities. This course uses selected concepts to plan the original recording; it does not decide an exception or certify the whole output. A clearly labeled media alternative for existing text is a defined condition, not a label an author can add to dismiss missing content without examining the actual relationship.

MNIT’s multimedia guidance encourages considering the message and accessibility during planning. Here, Elva can identify the three pieces before committing to a recording that relies on a silent pointing gesture or adds alternatives later without checking meaning. Appropriate production resources and actual publication arrangements still matter. The practice does not require a particular vendor, a new purchase or a change to a live DHS recording.

Privately name the speech, relevant sound and visual choices in the supplied account. Then explain why a transcript of only the spoken sentence would leave information missing. No software, hearing or vision disclosure, real video or public work product is required. The next lesson examines a caption error that changes the optional instruction into an apparent demand.

items.title: Follow the message across channels
items.body: The spoken instruction does not name the two visible choices. A word-for-word speech copy would therefore preserve one part and omit another. Elva can identify that gap early rather than assume every important part is already in the narrator’s sentence because the video is short.

items.title: Keep the media types distinct
items.body: Silent video does not contain speech to caption, while audio-only does not contain visuals to describe. The main recording contains both. Niko’s plan should fit the actual content rather than copy a single rule from another format and call the alternatives complete.

items.title: Retain actual scope
items.body: The selected media concepts help ask useful questions, but the full adopted standard and real responsibilities remain. Calling the recording practice or attaching an accessibility label does not authorize an exception. The learner can understand the content map without producing or releasing any media.

tabs.label: Only the spoken sentence
tabs.body: This account preserves the optional instruction but not the named visual choices or relevant transition. It could be a useful starting point, yet it is not the full message supplied for the exercise. Elva needs to identify what other meaningful information should be available through an appropriate alternative.

tabs.label: Only the visible card
tabs.body: This account preserves Timing and Wording but does not carry the spoken statement that no decision is needed today. A person could mistake the purpose if the remaining channel is assumed to supply itself. Keep the instruction and the choices connected rather than treating the card as the whole recording.

tabs.label: The three meaningful pieces
tabs.body: The content map identifies speech, question choices and the relevant transition sound. It provides a fitting basis for caption and description planning. It still does not show that files, timing, player operation or actual delivery have been completed; planning evidence and usable output remain different.

check.question: Which account describes the supplied message fully enough to plan its alternatives?
check.correct: The optional spoken instruction, the Timing and Wording choices and the relevant transition sound all need appropriate consideration.
wrong: The spoken sentence alone contains every supplied piece of information.
Any silent video must have speech captions even when it has no audio.
Calling the item practice automatically creates an accessibility exception.
check.feedbackCorrect: This starts with the actual content and retains the separate media and requirement questions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The spoken sentence omits the visible choices and supplied sound meaning. Silent video has no speech to caption. A practice label does not create an exception to requirements that apply to real content.

lessons.title: Check whether captions preserve the instruction
lessons.summary: A caption file needs to carry the relevant speech and sound accurately at the right time. One missing word can change what a person is asked to do.
lessons.objective: Identify how the supplied missing word changes the instruction.
objectives: Identify how the supplied missing word changes the instruction.
Distinguish accurate caption text from timing and complete-media results.
Choose a specific correction without declaring every automatic caption unusable.
takeaways: Relevant sound is part of the caption question.
Correcting text does not settle timing or the whole recording.
lessons.statement: Check what the captions tell the viewer, not just whether a caption option exists.

intro.heading: What changed when the word no disappeared?
intro.body:
The caption excerpt reads Decision is needed today; choose a question to discuss. The supplied speech says No decision is needed today; choose a question to discuss. Losing no reverses an important part of the instruction. Niko should not accept the excerpt merely because most words match or a caption symbol is visible. The relevant question is whether the person receiving the text gets the intended meaning.

The excerpt gives one specific correction: restore the negation so the discussion is not presented as requiring a decision today. It does not describe the accuracy of a real automated system or prove that every automatic caption is wrong. W3C explains that automatic captions can be a starting point but need their actual accuracy confirmed. The source’s concept supports checking this original excerpt rather than borrowing its examples or assuming the software performed the review.

Captioning also concerns relevant non-speech audio, not only dialogue. In the example, the chime marks the transition to a closing screen. The plan needs to consider how that sound’s relevant information is available in the captions. Niko should not give it an invented meaning such as approval granted or infer a speaker’s emotion. The content account supplies a transition, and the wording should stay within that role.

Timing is a separate question. Captions are synchronized with the audio, so a correct sentence displayed at the wrong point can still confuse the exchange. This exercise supplies the text mismatch but no measured timestamp or completed playback observation. Restoring no therefore resolves the selected text issue in the proposal, not the whole caption track. There is no basis to claim timing has passed or that every speaker and relevant sound is covered.

WCAG’s prerecorded-caption criterion has its own scope and specified exception; a plain transcript is not automatically the same as synchronized captions. Appropriate production work needs the actual output and delivery to be examined. Elva can retain a specific correction request, a relevant sound question and an open timing check without making a release decision or blaming a viewer for not understanding an inaccurate instruction.

Privately compare the supplied speech and text. Explain the change caused by no and identify the distinct timing question. You do not need to generate captions, upload a recording or claim that a real file has been repaired. The next lesson turns to the visual choices that were not named in the main spoken sentence.

lessons.keyStatement: A matching majority of words can still carry the wrong instruction.

accordion.heading: Examine the meaning and its presentation

items.title: Retain the negation
items.body: No determines whether a decision is needed today. The excerpt can contain many accurate words and still make the task misleading. Restoring this small word is therefore a meaningful correction, not cosmetic editing, and does not require inventing a different deadline or decision authority.

items.title: Name the relevant sound accurately
items.body: The content account gives the chime a transition role. Niko can preserve that information without making it mean approval or adding a reaction that the recording never supplies. A caption alternative should retain the relevant message rather than become commentary about what the author thinks the viewer should feel.

items.title: Keep timing open
items.body: The supplied comparison gives text, not a tested playback sequence. A correct revised sentence is a useful proposal, but it does not establish synchronization. Elva can name the next examination precisely rather than treat one correction as proof that every caption, speaker and sound has been handled.

tabs.label: The caption icon is visible
tabs.body: The icon indicates an available option, not accurate content. It does not answer what the caption says or when it appears. Niko needs to examine the selected excerpt so a present feature does not conceal the reversal of the optional instruction.

tabs.label: The intended sentence is restored
tabs.body: This proposal repairs the supplied missing negation. It is a specific improvement in meaning and can be reported as such. Relevant sound, speaker information, timing and the rest of the recording still need their own examination rather than inheriting success from the one sentence.

tabs.label: Every automatic caption is rejected
tabs.body: One invented mismatch cannot describe every tool or output. A fitting response uses the excerpt as a starting point for checking and correcting actual content. It avoids both automatic acceptance and a universal claim of uselessness while keeping the intended message central.

The visible caption option proves the text and timing are correct.
One invented mismatch proves all automatic captions are unusable.
check.feedbackCorrect: This identifies the specific meaning error and retains the limits of the supplied evidence.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The missing negation changes what is asked. An icon does not review content or timing. One practice excerpt cannot establish a universal result for every generated caption.

lessons.title: Make the important visual meaning available
lessons.summary: A spoken instruction can be clear while leaving a visual choice unexplained. Examine which information is missing and how a fitting description or transcript preserves it.
lessons.objective: Identify the important visual choices absent from the supplied narration.
objectives: Identify the important visual choices absent from the supplied narration.

intro.heading: Which questions can the listener choose?
intro.body:
The practice narration says choose a question to discuss but never names the two visible choices. The card contains Timing and Wording. A person relying on the main audio would receive an invitation to choose without receiving those supplied choices. This is a specific gap in the original content map. It does not establish why any actual viewer selected a question or describe the needs of a population.

Elva proposes adding The Questions card offers Timing and Wording to the main spoken explanation. That is an example of planning the important visual information into the narration. It identifies the card’s relevant meaning rather than describing every decorative detail. Niko does not need to add an inferred emotion or call one choice more responsible than the other. Neither interpretation is supplied by the recording.

W3C describes integrated description, separate described versions and player-supported description approaches. The fitting method depends on the actual content, timing and delivery. Elva’s proposed sentence is a script change, not a completed recording. It still needs to be included in the output and examined with the surrounding content. A written plan can identify the gap without proving that a person can obtain and use the described version.

A descriptive transcript has another purpose: it includes important visual information along with the speech and relevant sound in text. A speech-only transcript of the first sentence would omit Timing and Wording. Adding the relevant card information can make the text account more complete, but text availability is not automatically the same as an audio description result. In particular, the Level AA prerecorded audio-description criterion cannot be dismissed merely by attaching a text transcript to synchronized media with important visual information absent from the audio.

The adopted Minnesota standard and applicable WCAG conditions retain their actual scope. This selected practice is not a complete conformance review, and it does not authorize an exception. If all important visual information is already carried accurately in the main audio, that is a different content condition from this original missing-choice example. Examine the actual message rather than assume every talking-head recording needs the same added details or that every video is complete because words are spoken.

Privately write a short proposed sentence that conveys the supplied choices and identify what would remain to examine. You may keep the practice entirely textual and unrecorded. No actual film, audio track, transcript publication or disability disclosure is required. The next lesson examines two people’s learned ideas of faithfulness to a recording and care for a listener.

accordion.heading: Keep the description accurate and usable

items.title: Name the supplied choices
items.body: Timing and Wording are the information needed to understand this particular choice invitation. Elva’s proposed sentence can carry that meaning without inventorying ornamental details or adding a preferred answer. Keeping description tied to the task makes its purpose clear and avoids turning it into the author’s interpretation of a viewer’s feelings.

items.title: Distinguish the script from the output
items.body: A fitting sentence is an improvement to the proposal. Niko still needs actual production and delivery evidence before saying the description is available and works with the rest of the media. The learner can identify the script change without claiming a completed audio track or a player function that has not been examined.

items.title: Retain the different alternatives
items.body: A descriptive text account can preserve the card information, while an audio description makes it available through sound. Their roles are related but not identical. Keeping the applicable criterion clear prevents a useful transcript from being presented as an automatic substitute for every other required alternative.

tabs.label: Look at the card
tabs.body: This repeats reliance on sight rather than explaining the important choices. It can leave the listener at the same gap as before. Niko can replace the visual-only direction with the actual supplied names without assuming that the listener is unwilling to take part.

tabs.label: The card offers Timing and Wording
tabs.body: This proposal conveys the important missing meaning. It does not infer an emotion, a correct choice or an actual viewer response. The script and output still need relevant examination; a clear proposed sentence is not a completed recording or universal access result.

tabs.label: The responsible choice is Wording
tabs.body: This adds a value judgment the recording never supplies. It would alter the invitation rather than preserve it. Description should not quietly recommend an answer or claim that the author knows why a person chooses; the two supplied options remain open for discussion.

check.question: Which proposal preserves the missing visual meaning?
check.correct: Explain that the Questions card offers Timing and Wording, while retaining the output and applicable alternative requirements.
wrong: Say look at the card without naming either choice.
Add that responsible participants select Wording.
Declare a text transcript an automatic replacement for the relevant Level AA audio-description requirement.
check.feedbackCorrect: This carries the actual choices without adding a judgment or confusing a proposed sentence with complete delivery.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A visual-only direction does not convey the choices. A preferred-answer judgment changes the content. A text transcript has a useful role but does not automatically replace the applicable audio-description criterion.

The card offers Wording.

lessons.title: Learn what faithful explanation means to the listener
lessons.summary: Chosen personal accounts can reveal different learned meanings of faithfulness and care. A wider understanding can change a proposed explanation while preserving what the recording actually says.
lessons.objective: Identify the individual learned meanings supplied by Jude and Leila.
objectives: Identify the individual learned meanings supplied by Jude and Leila.
Explain how their accounts widen the first motive interpretation.
Choose a changed description proposal that preserves both meaning and accuracy.
takeaways: Faithfulness can have different learned meanings.
Understanding the other account can change the response.
A personal meaning does not become a group profile or an outcome claim.
lessons.statement: Ask what faithful communication means in this encounter rather than decide whose motive is deficient.

intro.heading: Why does one friend preserve the exact words while the other asks for context?
intro.body:
Consider Jude and Leila, two friends who choose to discuss a personal recording, separate from Elva’s draft video. Jude describes helping preserve a relative’s spoken stories. In that experience, keeping the person’s exact phrasing was learned as care: it prevented a later editor from replacing the speaker’s voice with their own account. Leila describes using museum audio guides where explaining an unfamiliar object’s relevant context was learned as care: it let a listener understand a reference rather than hear a word without its meaning.

Jude initially calls Leila’s request for explanation meddling. Leila initially calls Jude’s insistence on exact phrasing indifference to the listener. Their chosen accounts widen both interpretations. Jude is protecting the person’s voice; Leila is trying to make the relevant reference understandable. Neither account makes every editor accurate or every added explanation appropriate. Ask about each person’s experience rather than assuming their preferences come from a group identity.

They propose a changed approach for the personal recording. Preserve the quoted wording as the speaker’s words and make any fitting added explanation distinguishable from that quote. Leila can ask which reference needs context without inventing the relative’s intent. Jude can consider a useful explanation without treating every addition as replacement of the speaker’s voice. Actual permission and the source’s purpose remain relevant to any real recording; the example supplies a proposal, not publication or agreement from the original speaker.

Elva can learn from that distinction when describing her practice card. Naming Timing and Wording carries relevant visible content. Declaring that Wording is the responsible choice would add the author’s judgment. The friends’ accounts help her separate preserving a message from interpreting a person. They do not decide the technical method, create permission or replace the applicable requirements for a media output.

The Council of Europe discusses learning through individually contextual meanings, wider self-and-other understanding and fitting responses. Here the learning can be personal: Jude and Leila reconsider a motive label and a way to receive a request for explanation. No assessment position is inferred from their preferences, and no one must supply a personal story in order to finish the course.

Privately compare the first labels with the two chosen meanings and identify the specific changed proposal. You may keep your reflection unrecorded or use only the example. Understanding has value without producing an actual recording, proving that a group has changed or reporting a later listener outcome. The next lesson asks whether a proposed set of media alternatives can actually be obtained and operated through its delivery.

lessons.keyStatement: Preserving a voice and explaining a reference can both matter, with the distinction made clear.

flashcards.back: Exact phrasing can express care for the original speaker’s voice in his chosen account.
Relevant context can express care for understanding in her chosen account.
Meddling and indifference are the initial motive interpretations.
Retain the quote and distinguish fitting added explanation without inventing intent.
You can learn by considering another interpretation, without sharing a personal story or labeling anyone.

accordion.heading: Connect the meaning to a changed response

items.title: Protect the speaker without closing inquiry
items.body: Jude’s account explains why he resists replacing the relative’s language. Leila can take that concern seriously rather than assign indifference. They can still examine whether a reference needs additional explanation, with the original quote and any fitting addition made distinguishable rather than silently rewriting the speaker’s message.

items.title: Explain without inventing intent
items.body: Leila’s account explains why a bare unfamiliar word may not satisfy her listening task. Jude can ask what context would be useful instead of assigning meddling. The proposed explanation should remain tied to the actual reference, because care for understanding does not establish authority to invent what the speaker meant or felt.

items.title: Carry the distinction into the practice card
items.body: Elva can name the supplied visual choices while avoiding the invented responsible-answer judgment. The personal encounter changes how she understands the difference between explanation and interpretation. It does not establish a production result, approval or an automatic rule for every recording, and personal insight remains useful.

tabs.heading: Compare three responses to the encounter

tabs.label: Choose a deficient motive
tabs.body: Calling Jude indifferent or Leila meddling prevents the chosen meanings from shaping the response. Their accounts supply another way to understand the disagreement. Neither initial label is an established fact about the person, so replacing it with inquiry can improve the proposal without claiming certainty about every intention.

tabs.label: Hear the individual meanings
tabs.body: The family-story and museum-guide experiences explain why the two friends value different aspects of faithful communication. These are contextual accounts, not universal group traits or diagnosis. They support wider understanding while keeping each person’s actual choice and the original recording’s information distinct.

tabs.label: Distinguish quotation and explanation
tabs.body: The changed proposal preserves the speaker’s words and makes a fitting added explanation identifiable. This responds to both concerns rather than erase either. Permission, accuracy and later listener use remain open in the example; the proposal is meaningful learning without being a completed media release or outcome.

check.question: What learning follows from the two chosen accounts?
check.correct: They can reconsider the motive labels and propose a clear distinction between the speaker’s words and fitting added explanation.
wrong: Jude’s preference proves everyone from his family rejects context.
Leila’s wish for context permits any invented explanation of the speaker’s intent.
The proposal establishes that the original speaker approved publication.
check.feedbackCorrect: This uses contextual meaning to change the response without a group prediction, invented intent or permission claim.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Jude’s chosen experience is not a family profile. Leila’s meaning does not authorize invention. The example supplies neither the original speaker’s approval nor a completed publication.

sorting.heading: Separate the chosen meaning, changed proposal and unsupported inference

items.text: Jude connects exact phrasing with care for the speaker’s voice.
Leila connects relevant context with care for a listener’s understanding.
Keep the original quote distinct from fitting explanation.

The proposal proves a later listener understood.

lessons.transfer: Privately identify how wider understanding changes a proposed response without turning it into a universal media rule.

move.failure: An individual account becomes a group prediction or permission to invent a speaker’s intent.

lessons.title: Examine the delivered content and controls
lessons.summary: Accurate alternatives need a usable delivery route. A player’s reputation and a file saved elsewhere do not supply evidence that a person can find and operate the relevant content.
lessons.objective: Identify the three supplied player-task observations.
objectives: Identify the three supplied player-task observations.
Distinguish an existing caption file from an operable caption control.
Choose a specific delivery inquiry without relaxing actual security or publication arrangements.
takeaways: Content and controls need their own examination.
A stored file is not completed delivery.

lessons.statement: Follow the alternative through the actual delivery rather than stop at the file.

intro.heading: Can the proposed alternatives be reached?
intro.body:
For this example, Niko looks at three observations of a prototype player. Using the supplied keyboard path, a tester starts playback. The same path does not reach the caption control. A separately labeled transcript link opens the supplied text account. Focus on what these three observations tell us and what the team still needs to check.

The three observations answer different questions. Starting playback shows one operation along the supplied path. The unreachable caption control identifies a specific delivery barrier to examine. Opening the transcript shows that the link reaches the supplied account under those conditions; it does not establish that the text preserves all content, has appropriate structure or replaces the required media alternatives. Niko should retain each observation rather than report one overall success based on playback alone.

W3C’s player guidance identifies operation without a mouse, visible focus, meaningful control labels and related interface considerations. MNIT’s multimedia guidance also connects player use with caption and description availability. A tool advertised as accessible still needs relevant examination in its actual configuration and content. The example supplies no brand-specific verdict, comprehensive control test or permission to alter an approved platform.

Suppose Elva has a revised caption file saved in a work folder. That file’s existence does not answer whether the delivery connects it to the correct recording or lets a viewer use it. Likewise, a described version stored separately needs an appropriate way to be obtained. A useful question follows the alternative through the actual content, link and player arrangement rather than assume the production file and the delivered experience are identical.

The caption-control issue may need the relevant technical support and actual authoring responsibilities. Niko should not loosen security settings, expose a restricted file or publish an unreviewed copy elsewhere as an automatic workaround. Actual information, publication and procurement arrangements retain their role. Describing a barrier accurately supports a fitted inquiry; it does not grant new authority over a platform or decide an individual assistance need.

Privately write the three-task account and identify the question raised by the unreachable control. You do not need to test a real player, install software or provide individual information. You can use the example to practice separating content quality, operation and delivery. The final lesson returns to the full recording account and identifies what its proposed corrections still do not prove.

The labeled link opens the supplied text account under the defined conditions.
Production material whose connection to delivered content still needs examination.
Ask about the specific control and delivery arrangement without creating an unauthorized workaround.

accordion.heading: Connect the production work to use

items.title: Retain the control barrier
items.body: Niko cannot report the player as fully operable from a successful start command when the caption control remains unreachable along the same path. The specific observation helps the relevant support examine the intended function. It does not establish that every control fails or identify the tester’s health or ability.

items.title: Keep text quality separate
items.body: The transcript link opens, which is useful delivery evidence. Its content still needs to preserve the relevant speech, sound and visual information for its purpose. Treating a successful link as a full media result would conceal both the caption-control issue and any unexamined text content.

items.title: Follow the actual version
items.body: A revised file saved elsewhere needs to be connected with the intended recording and available through the appropriate route. Version and configuration matter to the result. Elva can identify those questions without moving restricted information to an unapproved location or assuming that a platform’s advertised features are active.

tabs.label: Playback starts
tabs.body: This is a specific supplied operation result. It shows progress in one task but leaves the caption control unresolved and the rest of the interface unexamined. Reporting the whole player as accessible would extend a local observation beyond the content and conditions actually supplied.

tabs.label: The caption control is not reached
tabs.body: This is a specific barrier in the defined prototype path. A useful inquiry concerns that function and its actual delivery. It does not prove that all captions are inaccurate or justify dropping them, publishing elsewhere without authority or blaming a viewer for the inaccessible route.

tabs.label: The transcript link opens
tabs.body: The route reaches the supplied text account, which differs from verifying its completeness and structure. The result can be retained without pretending it replaces synchronized captions or audio description. A useful account keeps content quality, media requirements and local operation evidence distinct.

check.question: Which account fits the three supplied observations?
check.correct: Playback starts, the caption control is not reached through the defined path and the transcript account opens, with wider results still unexamined.
wrong: Playback starts, so every player operation is verified.
Opening the transcript eliminates the caption-control issue and every other media requirement.
The control issue automatically authorizes publishing the recording on any other platform.
check.feedbackCorrect: This uses each actual observation and leaves the appropriate content, function and authority questions visible.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A start command does not test every function. The transcript’s link result does not repair the caption control or replace every required alternative. A barrier does not grant new publication or platform authority.

sorting.heading: Separate supplied operation, useful inquiry and unsupported judgment

items.text: The defined keyboard path starts playback.
The labeled transcript link opens the supplied account.
Ask why the caption control is not reached along that path.
Examine how the revised file connects to the intended delivered recording.
Every control is verified because playback starts.
Any alternate publication route is automatically authorized.

lessons.next: Return the whole account as specific progress, proposals and open checks.

scenario.context: Elva has the three prototype observations. Niko wants to mark delivery complete because playback starts and a transcript link opens, despite the unreachable caption control.
options: The whole player and media are verified.
Retain the successful operations and identify the specific caption-control inquiry, without inventing full results or workaround authority.
Delete the caption plan because one control was not reached.
responses: That exceeds the observations and omits a supplied barrier.
This preserves progress and the real next question while keeping actual responsibilities.
A delivery issue does not remove the relevant caption purpose or establish a legitimate exception.

lessons.transfer: Use the supplied operation account to distinguish files, controls and delivery without performing a real platform change.

move.control: Retain each observation and fit the next question to the unresolved function.
move.failure: A local success becomes complete certification or a barrier becomes unauthorized workaround permission.
move.next: You may privately describe the three tasks and one fitted inquiry; no installation, actual tester data or live publication is required.

lessons.title: Return the message, progress and open checks
lessons.summary: A useful media account states what was supplied, what a proposal changes and which results remain unknown. It can guide follow-through without turning optional practice into a live production requirement.
lessons.objective: Summarize the supplied instruction, choices and transition accurately.
objectives: Summarize the supplied instruction, choices and transition accurately.
Distinguish proposed content corrections from verified delivered media.
Choose a next account that preserves missing information and actual responsibilities.
takeaways: The message remains the reference point.
A correction proposal is not a completed output.
Specific progress and open checks can be reported together.
lessons.statement: Keep the content’s meaning and the evidence’s limits clear in the return.

image.caption: Two people hold an open document while one points to a line on the page.

intro.heading: What can Elva say has improved?
intro.body:
The complete practice record begins with a spoken optional instruction, two visual question choices and a relevant transition sound. The supplied caption excerpt omits no and reverses the instruction. Elva proposes restoring that meaning, considering the relevant sound and naming Timing and Wording in the main explanation. The personal Jude/Leila encounter widens the interpretation of faithful communication and leads to a proposal to distinguish original wording from fitting added explanation. The prototype account supplies playback and transcript-link successes along with an unreachable caption control.

These are useful pieces, but they are not a completed accessible recording. No final caption timing, recorded integrated description, complete output review or revised player-task response is supplied. The next prototype’s caption-control result is unknown. Recording it as successful because a fix is planned would invent evidence; recording it as zero or deliberate refusal would also invent information that is absent.

Elva can return an accurate account: The exercise identified a missing negation and visual choices absent from the main audio. Specific correction proposals are available. One supplied keyboard path starts playback but does not reach the caption control, and the labeled transcript link opens. Relevant content, timing and corrected delivery still need examination. This recognizes progress without concealing the unresolved function or treating one text link as complete media conformance.

The next inquiry can fit the open issue. Does the delivered revision retain the instruction and the choices? Are the captions accurate and synchronized? Does the intended route provide the necessary alternatives and usable controls? Those are questions, not a new universal schedule, a guarantee of improved service outcomes or permission to publish. Actual technical, editorial, assistance, information and authority responsibilities remain with their appropriate roles.

The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program and provides guidance, knowledge and feedback. Staff own their work and can use support without a new mandatory consultant gate for every media choice. Actual DHS daily equity responsibilities and qualifying formal-analysis procedures remain separate from this optional exercise. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA rather than taught through the general recording case.

Learning is voluntary. You can finish with the full example, a suitable draft or private reflection. No real video, production purchase, disability disclosure, recording of a person or public reflection is required. Personal insight and a more accurate account are useful learning, even when the next technical result remains open.

inThisLesson: The supplied message and identified gaps
lessons.keyStatement: An honest return can recognize progress and retain what is still unexamined.

flashcards.back: Optional discussion instruction, Timing and Wording choices and a transition sound.
The supplied caption omits no; the main narration omits the named choices.
Restore meaning and consider an appropriate integrated explanation; no final output is supplied.
Playback starts and the transcript link opens, while the caption control is not reached through the defined path.
No revised caption-control response is supplied; the result is not zero or guaranteed success.

accordion.heading: Make the return accurate and useful

items.title: Recognize the specific progress
items.body: The content map and correction proposals make the task clearer. Elva can explain the missing negation and absent choices without claiming that the recording has been produced or released. This gives a next reader usable information about what to examine rather than a vague statement that accessibility has been handled.

items.title: Keep the missing result visible
items.body: The next control response has not been supplied. Retaining that absence prevents a planned correction from becoming a success statistic or an invented failure. The existing prototype barrier still matters, while the next version requires its own evidence rather than inheriting a result from intention.

items.title: Keep learning and actual work distinct
items.body: A learner can understand the content and evidence distinctions through the example. Real media work retains applicable requirements, permissions and responsibilities. Neither private reflection nor course completion certifies a recording, creates an exception or requires a live production project to prove that the learning counts.

tabs.label: Everything has been made accessible
tabs.body: This claim treats proposals and selected operation observations as a complete result. It hides unexamined timing, recording and next-control information. Elva can recognize the useful work while explaining exactly which results still need evidence, rather than give the reader reassurance stronger than the supplied account.

tabs.label: Nothing useful occurred
tabs.body: This dismisses the meaningful content findings, changed personal interpretation and specific known operations. An unresolved control does not erase those pieces. The account can retain both progress and the remaining barrier without forcing a whole-success or whole-failure judgment.

tabs.label: Specific findings and fitted next questions
tabs.body: This account identifies the instruction error, visual gap, proposals and local operation evidence, then names what remains open. It supports appropriate follow-through without claiming causation, approval or a universal outcome. It also permits genuine private learning without collecting actual recordings or making a public proof requirement.

check.question: Which return follows the complete practice record?
check.correct: State the specific content gaps, correction proposals and operation observations, while retaining timing, output and next-control results as open.
wrong: Record the next caption-control result as successful because a correction is planned.
Treat the missing next result as zero or deliberate refusal.
Reject all personal learning because no live video was produced.
check.feedbackCorrect: This recognizes actual information and useful learning without converting proposals or absent evidence into results.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A plan is not a supplied test result. Missing information is neither zero nor a motive. Thinking it through can help, even when you choose to keep your response private.

sorting.heading: Separate supplied findings, open checks and unsupported closing claims

items.text: The original caption omits no.
The prototype path starts playback but does not reach the caption control.
The final recording’s timing is not supplied.
The next caption-control response remains unknown.
A proposed correction establishes full media conformance.
No live production means no meaningful learning occurred.

lessons.next: Retain the learning privately or carry a specific question into suitable work through its actual responsibilities.

scenario.context: Niko wants a final return. He has the content map, proposals and prototype observations but no produced revision or next control result.
scenario.prompt: Which return is useful and accurate?
options: Everything is verified because a plan exists.
The missing next result is proof of a person’s refusal.
Describe the supplied findings and known operations, then identify the open content and delivery questions through their appropriate roles.
responses: An intention does not supply the missing output or control evidence.
Missing information does not establish motive or an operation result.
This recognizes progress and preserves the real questions without inventing approval, conformance or a personal inference.

lessons.transfer: Write or privately consider a clear account of supplied meaning, proposals, known operations and open checks.

move.control: Use the content and evidence to guide a specific next inquiry.
move.failure: Proposals, missing results or optional learning are turned into certification, motive claims or compulsory live work.
move.next: Explore the example or reflect privately, at your own pace.

jobAid.title: Preserve the media message and examine its delivery
jobAid.subtitle: Keep content, alternative proposals, local operations and open checks in one accurate account.

sections.heading: Map the important message
items: The original practice speech says no decision is needed today. The Questions card names Timing and Wording; the chime marks the transition. Speech alone does not supply the complete content account.

Audio-only, silent video and synchronized audio-video have different content and alternative questions. Actual criteria, conditions and exceptions retain their scope; an author’s practice label creates no waiver.

sections.heading: Examine the caption meaning
items: The supplied excerpt drops no and reverses the instruction. Restore that meaning in the proposal without claiming the entire track has been verified.

Consider relevant non-speech sound and synchronization. The caption icon is not accuracy evidence, and a selected text correction provides no timing result or universal judgment about automatic output.

sections.heading: Explain relevant visual information
items: Timing and Wording are the missing visual choices. A fitting main-audio proposal names them without adding a responsible-answer judgment or guessing intent.

A descriptive transcript preserves relevant visual information along with audio in text. It is useful but is not an automatic substitute for the applicable AA audio-description requirement when important visual meaning is absent from main audio. Content, method, timing and actual delivery remain questions.

sections.heading: Learn from the personal meanings
items: Jude’s chosen relative-story account connects exact phrasing with care for the speaker’s voice. Leila’s chosen museum-guide account connects relevant context with care for the listener. Those accounts widen the original meddling/indifference labels.

Their changed proposal keeps quoted words distinct from fitting added explanation. No original-speaker permission, group profile, personal assessment or later listener result is supplied. You can learn from this without making a recording.

sections.heading: Follow the delivered alternatives
items: The complete practice keyboard path starts playback but does not reach the caption control. The labeled transcript link opens the supplied account. These are three different limited task observations.

A saved production file still needs the fitting connection to its intended recording and delivery. Content quality, controls and actual configuration are different inquiries. A barrier does not authorize security relaxation, unrestricted sharing or an unapproved platform change.

sections.heading: Return the known and open information
items: Describe the supplied gaps, proposals and local operations specifically. Final caption timing, recorded description, complete review and the next control response are not supplied; missing results are not zero, success or a motive.
Fit next inquiries to actual content, technical, assistance, editorial and agency responsibilities. The exercise makes no full conformance, release, causal or service-outcome claim.

The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program and provides guidance, knowledge and feedback. Staff own their work and can use support without a new mandatory consultant gate for every choice. Actual DHS formal analysis remains; Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.

remember: A recording, a caption icon, a text file and one successful operation are different evidence. Preserve the message and the actual conditions of each finding.
Explore the example or reflect privately, at your own pace.

sources.title: MNIT: Multimedia accessibility
sources.note: Connects planning the message with captions, visual description, transcripts and player use. Its reminders support a fitted inquiry and do not constitute a comprehensive or platform-specific test.

sources.title: WCAG 2.1: Time-based media
sources.note: Distinguishes prerecorded and live media, audio-only and video-only content, relevant alternatives, levels and specified exceptions. The selected practice does not certify the entire output or create an exception.

sources.title: W3C: Captions and subtitles
sources.note: Explains accurate speech and relevant sound text with synchronization. The original missing-negation exercise examines meaning without treating an icon or generated text as verified output.

sources.title: W3C: Description of visual information
sources.note: Explains meaningful visual description and delivery methods fitted to content, timing and player support. Naming the original question choices is a proposal, not completed audio or conformance evidence.

sources.title: W3C: Transcripts
sources.note: Distinguishes basic and descriptive text accounts and their relevant media uses. A text link and accurate content remain different questions, and a transcript is not automatically every required media alternative.

sources.title: W3C: Media players
sources.note: Connects accessible operations, meaningful controls and alternative delivery. The three original prototype observations remain limited to their supplied tasks rather than a brand or whole-player verdict.

sources.title: Minnesota State Digital Accessibility Standard
sources.note: Sets adopted digital requirements and their scope, responsibilities and exceptions. Optional media practice does not replace applicable review or authorize a release.

sources.title: DHS: Content and writing guidelines
sources.note: Supports preserving purpose, task information and accurate status in a clear account. Intended corrections, supplied findings and unknown results remain distinct.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Supports learning through contextual meanings and a changed response. Jude’s and Leila’s original chosen accounts are individual explanations, not group profiles, required disclosures or formal assessments.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Sets daily equity responsibilities and qualifying formal-analysis procedures. The optional recording exercises retain the actual toolkit or relevant customized-tool requirements.
